cards: Ashurbanipal was king of the Assyrian Empire from 669 to 627 BCE, the last great Assyrian ruler.
Sennacherib was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BCE, known for rebuilding Nineveh as a magnificent capital.
Cyaxares was king of the Medes in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BCE and the main architect of the Median Empire.
Necho II was a pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-sixth Dynasty in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BCE.
Josiah was king of Judah from about 640 to 609 BCE.
reigned c. 640–609 BCE · Ancient Near East
Duke Huan of Qi ruled the state of Qi in eastern China from 685 to 643 BCE.
Gyges was king of Lydia from around 680 BCE and founder of the Mermnad dynasty.
Periander was tyrant of Corinth from about 627 to 587 BCE, son and successor of Cypselus.
Psamtik I was the founder of Egypt's Twenty-sixth, or Saite, Dynasty, reigning from 664 to 610 BCE.
Colaeus was a Samian merchant whose voyage is told by Herodotus.
Duke Mu of Qin ruled the State of Qin from 659 to 621 BCE and is often listed among the Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period.
Guan Zhong was chief minister of the State of Qi under Duke Huan from 685 BCE until his death in 645 BCE.
Archilochus was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Paros, active in the 7th century BCE and regarded in antiquity as the master of iambic verse.
Candaules was the last king of the Heraclid dynasty of Lydia, killed around 680 BCE by Gyges, who founded the Mermnad dynasty.
d. c. 680 BCE · Ancient Near East
Humban-haltash III was the last known king of Elam.
Jehoiakim was king of Judah from 609 to 598 BCE, a son of Josiah.
Taharqa was a king of Kush and pharaoh of Egypt of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the seventh century BCE, one of the most powerful Kushite rulers.
Battus I was the founder and first king of Cyrene in Libya, who, according to Herodotus, led settlers from the island of Thera there around 631 BCE on the advice of the Delphic oracle.
Duke Wen of Jin, born Chong'er, spent nineteen years in exile among other states before taking the throne of Jin in 636 BCE.
Duke Xian of Jin was ruler of the state of Jin in northern China during the Spring and Autumn period.
Teumman was king of Elam from about 664 to 653 BCE.
Aristomenes is the legendary hero of the Messenians, said to have led their revolt against Sparta in the Second Messenian War in the 7th century BCE.
Draco was an Athenian legislator who about 621 BCE gave Athens its first written code of laws, replacing oral law and blood feud administered by the aristocracy.
Ikausu was a king of the Philistine city of Ekron in the early 7th century BCE and son of King Padi; his name corresponds to the biblical Achish.
King Cheng of Chu ruled the southern Chinese state of Chu from 671 to 626 BCE.
King Zhuang of Chu (reigned 613–591 BCE) was a ruler of the State of Chu, counted among the Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period.
Necho I was a ruler of Sais in the western Nile Delta in the 7th century BCE and the father of Psamtik I, founder of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.
Perdiccas I is named by Herodotus as the founder of the Argead royal house of Macedon in the 7th century BCE.
Tullus Hostilius was the third of the legendary kings of Rome, traditionally reigning from 673 to 642 BCE.
Zaleucus was the lawgiver of Locri Epizephyrii in southern Italy, credited with drawing up the first written Greek law code in the mid-7th century BCE.
Amon was king of Judah for about two years in the mid-7th century BCE, the son and successor of Manasseh.
Jehoahaz was king of Judah for three months in 609 BCE, a son of Josiah.
Manasseh was king of Judah for about half a century in the 7th century BCE, the son of Hezekiah.
Tyrtaeus was a Greek elegiac poet who lived in Sparta in the mid-seventh century BCE, during the Second Messenian War.
